# The Number on the Bottom of the Bottle Was Never Talking to You

*A resin sorting code spent decades dressed as a recycling promise, and the costume did the work.*

Turn over almost any plastic container and you will find a small triangle with a number inside it, molded into the base. Ask what it means and most people will give the same answer: it means the thing can be recycled. In one survey, 68% of Americans thought anything labeled with the code could be recycled. They are wrong, and not because they are careless readers. They are wrong because the mark was designed for someone else entirely, and for decades it wore a costume that invited exactly this mistake.

The mark is a resin identification code. The Society of the Plastics Industry developed it in 1988 to give recyclers and manufacturers a consistent, worldwide way of saying which plastic resin an item is made of. The numbers run 1 to 7; the lower ones each name a specific resin, and the last is a catch-all for everything else. The purpose of the system is sorting. Recycling only works when a stream of material is chemically uniform, so the people handling bales of mixed plastic need a fast way to tell one polymer from another and keep them apart. ASTM International, which maintains the standard today, is blunt about the scope: the code identifies resin content. It says nothing about whether a product is recyclable, and it never did.

What turned an industrial inventory mark into a public promise was the picture around it. The number originally sat inside the chasing arrows, the looping triangle everyone recognizes as the recycling symbol. Read as a whole, the mark looked like a certification. It was nothing of the kind; it was a materials label wearing recycling's face. And the mark did not spread on merit alone. State laws required the codes on plastic packaging, in 39 states by Scientific American's count and 36 states by GreenBlue's, so the recycling-shaped stamp ended up on products regardless of whether any facility on earth would accept them.

Here is my reading of who got what out of that. A uniform code genuinely helped recyclers and manufacturers, and that need was real. But the graphic handed the plastics business something extra: every item, whether a bottle with a healthy end market or a tub nobody would ever reprocess, displayed a symbol the public associates with environmental responsibility. A shopper hesitating over a plastic purchase saw arrows and felt reassured. Whether anyone planned that effect is a separate question; the benefit was collected either way, item by item, for decades.

Was the costume deliberate? The published histories do not establish intent, and I will not invent it. What they do establish is the correction, and the correction is telling: in 2013, ASTM published a rule replacing the chasing arrows around the numbers with a plain solid triangle, precisely to separate the resin code from the recycling message. The fix has limits of its own. Manufacturers are not required to rework their labels, and the chasing arrows still appear on many products. The costume was retired by rule and kept in circulation by inertia.

The gap between the mark's official meaning and its street meaning is not cosmetic. Only 9% of plastics ever produced have gone on to be recycled, a figure that sits strangely beside a marking regime in which nearly every plastic item carries recycling's silhouette. California has moved against the gap with a truth-in-labeling law built around access: under it, 60% of Californians need access to a processing center. My reading of that design is that it forces a label to answer for real capacity rather than for a shape stamped in a mold, which is exactly the accountability the original mark never had to provide.

The date printed on a carton of milk does the same work. It is, at bottom, a stock-rotation signal, a note from the supply chain to the retailer about when to pull an item from the shelf. The shopper reads it as a safety deadline, a chemical fact about the milk, because the number is printed where the shopper is looking and nothing on the package says whom it is addressed to. The anatomy matches the resin code precisely: a figure generated by and for an industry's internal logistics, stamped onto the consumer-facing surface because that is where printing goes, and received by the household as a message about the household's own interests.

My suspicion is that this class of misreading survives for a simple reason: it costs the sender nothing, and the receiver has no way to audit it. The grocer loses little when a family treats a rotation date as a poison warning; the resin maker lost nothing when a shopper treated a sorting code as an environmental pledge. Correction arrives only when a body with authority over the mark itself steps in, as ASTM did with the graphic, and even then, as the surviving chasing arrows show, a rule about future labels does little about the millions already molded and printed. A misunderstanding that must be fixed by the party who benefits from it tends to have a long life; a misunderstanding that must be fixed by the party confused by it lasts longer still.

Nothing in the number tells you what your own curbside program will take; a code identifies a resin, not a destination, and local recyclability is a separate question the mark cannot answer. Why some items skip the code entirely, even when they appear to be the same resin, is only partly explained by the patchwork of state mandates. Why the less common resins lack workable recycling markets is stated in the published accounts only in outline, as a matter of low value and missing end markets. Whether the solid triangle will actually reduce the confusion is unknown, since the old arrows remain in wide circulation. And what happens to any particular coded container once it leaves your hand, recycled, burned or buried, the code cannot say and nothing on the package tracks.

The beneficiary of the original design has a name. The Society of the Plastics Industry built the code, and every product that wore the arrows borrowed the moral shine of recycling whatever its actual fate. The households sorting their bins by a number that was never addressed to them, and the local programs handling whatever arrives, carry the cost of the confusion. The industry that molded the arrows into the plastic was spared it.
